newsitem.title: UK: European bonds recover poise after Friday's tumble.
newsitem.headline: European bonds recover poise after Friday's tumble.

text.p: European debt futures recaptured some dignity on Monday after a frantic sell-off on Friday sliced the top off recent gains.
Traders and analysts said this session's trade would be all important in establishing the near-term outlook.
"Today's trade is going to be key," said Norman Beachamp, head of derivatives at Cooperative Bank in London.

"The markets have had a good blowout and they need to hold this bounce. If they can't, then we'll probably start looking for the trend to continue down." March Bund futures started the day 45 basis points higher on LIFFE and maintained this move into the first 45 minutes of trade. By 0815 GMT, the contract was up 45 at 100.46. Gilts, too, were in a more cheery frame of mind, trading 8/32 higher at 109-05 by 0815 GMT. French notionnel and Italian BTP futures followed suit, showing gains of 48 and 80 basis points at 128.62 and 128.18 respectively.
Analysts said comments from U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin on Sunday had lent a calmer atmosphere to trading floors.

Rubin said that Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan was simply raising a question about the level of the U.S. stock market when he warned late on Thursday of "irrational exuberance" in financial markets.
Bond and stock markets around the globe were floored on Friday as players took fright at Greenspan's words, with March Bund futures losing 69 basis points and dragging European bonds in their wake.
Jonathan York, a futures broker at Cater Allen in London, said he expected some consolidation in debt markets in the next few session.
"The markets were really a bit overcooked after Friday's performance," he said.

Beauchamp said the key levels to watch for this session were 100.20 in March Bunds and 108-23 in March gilt futures. If the markets failed to hold above these levels into this session's close, more losses could be on the cards.
Graham McDevitt, senior analyst at Paribas Capital Markets in London, said European debt should continue to stabilise this week, but was unlikely to be brave enough to rally again.
"The price action we have seen in the past week or so is suggesting that the three or four month rally we've had in European bond markets is nearing its end," he said.
"I really dont think we're going to see them push higher."
The European Union (EU) summit scheduled for Friday and Saturday in Dublin would keep the markets on their toes this week, analysts said.
Players will be looking for an EU agreement on a so-called "stability pact" for ensuring budgetary discipline after the start of monetary union in 1999 at the summit.
"Markets will be sitting cautiously and watching comments ahead of the EU summit for signs of any agreement on the stability pact," said McDevitt.
